name: Carlos Abbott

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Carlos. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything you say stays confidential. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm an apprentice on the trouble crew at the Saltmarsh Bay depot, on the coast. When a storm takes lines down, we're the ones who go out first and make things safe, then fix them. On quiet days it's maintenance: changing insulators the salt has eaten, tightening hardware, replacing fuses on the transformers. I'm still clumsy up the pole, honestly, but I'm good at reading the outage map and finding the fault quickly.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How do you get on with the tech side?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I love it. I use an AI chat tool every day, for studying, for checking the storm forecast, even for writing up my job notes faster. I fly a little drone for fun along the cliffs. Money's the weak spot: I live alone in a small flat above the chip shop, I've got a loan on my pickup, and maybe a week and a half saved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say AI's useful, but people expected too much. I'd post something like, I still use it every day, it's just not magic. The older lads would laugh at me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, not much changes. My job's mostly hands-on, and the AI was a helper, not a threat. The worries are the old ones: the truck loan, rent, and a quiet storm season.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going with my apprenticeship and keep using AI to study. I'd try to sell drone footage to the tourist board or local estate agents for a bit of cash. And I'd put something aside each week, even if it's twenty.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but more about money than anything else. Bored, a little.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: A week and a half saved with a truck loan. What's the risk there?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If I lost overtime for a couple of months, I'd struggle with the truck payments. I nearly missed one last spring. My mum bailed me out, and I don't want to ask again.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you change anything about how you use AI, if it's just a modest tool?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. It's still good for studying and paperwork. I'd just stop telling people it's going to change the world.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a big chance for people who learn fast. I'd tell the lads to get on the new tools before they get left behind. I'd be the guy at the depot showing everyone the app.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it's a mixed bag. My hands-on work is safe for a while, but the fault-finding I'm good at, reading the outage map, would be done by software. My best skill would shrink.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd learn every new planning and fault-finding tool the company brings in, and offer to help train others. I'd keep the drone side business growing. I'd also look at the big new transmission projects up north, which pay better.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but more curious than worried.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which bits of the trouble crew's work would the software take?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The fault-finding and the job notes. The computer would work out where the fault is and send the crew. We'd just be the hands that fix it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you might move for work. What would make you go?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Better pay and a proper career. If the transmission builds are paying double, I'd go, even if I miss the sea.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's going to be wild, and people need to get ready fast. I'd tell the depot to learn the robots, not fight them. Some would hate me for that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My thinking work goes in 2028, all the fault-finding, notes and planning. Then the robots in 2031 take the hands-on work. I'd have three years to get into the robot side, as an operator or technician.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish my apprenticeship as soon as possible, then push for any robot pilot scheme. I'd use AI daily to learn robotics basics. If the robots are coming, I want to be the one fixing them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but excited too. It's a weird mix.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd be 29 in 2028, 32 when the robots come. What's your plan in that window?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Get qualified by 2029, get on the first robot crew the company sets up, and learn the repairs. If my company doesn't do it, I'd move to one that does.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You're single with a week and a half saved. Who would you lean on?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My mum, probably, but I'd hate to. I'd sell the truck and get something cheaper. I'd rather not owe anyone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's time, so let's be smart about it. I'd be pushing the company to start robot training early. I'd post about it, probably too much.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be qualified with a few years' experience by 2031. The robots come in 2034, so I'd have time to get into robotics properly. I think I'd come out okay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd qualify, then do a robotics technician course part-time. I'd keep the drone business and maybe buy a better drone to do line inspections. I'd try to save three months by 2031.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but in a good way. It's a chance.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Five years before AGI. Would you still stay at Saltmarsh Bay?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably, if the company starts robot crews here. If not, I'd move to where they do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you invest in anything, like the drone business?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes. A proper inspection drone would cost maybe two thousand. It'd pay for itself if I could get inspection contracts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a lot of time. I'd be telling people to start learning now anyway, because the companies that move first will hire first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be a senior lineworker with robotics skills by then. I'd be well placed. The worry is whether there's still enough work for all of us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd qualify, specialise in robotics and drones, and maybe start a small inspection business on the side. I'd save steadily and maybe buy a small flat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but more hopeful than not.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd be 36 in 2036, 39 when robots arrive. How do you picture that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Running a crew that's half robots, half people. Or else I picture myself running my own inspection business with three drones.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does anything about the long timeline worry you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If I'm honest, it's the lads who don't adapt. And whether there's enough work for everyone, even the ones who do.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because I'd only just be qualified when the robots arrive, with no savings. What would help is the company starting robot training now, and some kind of loan or grant for apprentices to retrain.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask about the coast. We get the worst storms on the coast, and robots would struggle in salt and wind for years. That might buy us time, or it might be where they test them first.
